faqs.answer: About an hour on the counter is enough. Faster: put the eggs in a bowl of warm tap water for 5 to 10 minutes. Do not leave refrigerated eggs out for more than 2 hours; that is the USDA limit for perishable food at room temperature.
faqs.question: How long does it take eggs to reach room temperature?

faqs.answer: Yes, within limits. The USDA says refrigerated eggs should not be left out for more than 2 hours, or 1 hour when it is above 90°F (32°C). An hour on the counter to warm up is well inside that. Do not leave them out all day.
faqs.question: Is it safe to leave eggs out to warm up?

faqs.answer: Yes, about a minute and a quarter for a large egg. Hard-boiled goes from 10 minutes 10 seconds from the fridge to 8 minutes 55 seconds at room temperature. Soft goes from 4 minutes 30 seconds to 3 minutes 20 seconds.
faqs.question: Do room-temperature eggs really save time?

faqs.answer: Yes. A fridge-cold egg dropped into boiling water gets a sudden shock as the shell warms unevenly and the air pocket inside expands. A room-temperature egg warms more gently, so the shell is less likely to crack.
faqs.question: Do room-temperature eggs crack less?

faqs.answer: Only by seconds. Room temperature here means about 20°C, the convention Williams and most calculators use. A kitchen a few degrees warmer or cooler moves the time by seconds, not minutes, so the room setting still applies.
faqs.question: What if my kitchen is warmer or cooler than 20°C?

parts.meaning: The constant from the egg's thermal properties: density 1.038 g per cubic cm, specific heat 3.7, thermal conductivity 0.0054.
The weight of the egg in grams. A large egg is 57 g (USDA size).
The starting temperature of the egg: 20°C at room temperature, against 4°C from the fridge.
The boiling point of the water: 100°C at sea level, lower at altitude.
The target temperature at the edge of the yolk: 84°C for hard-boiled.
The yolk edge factor. The yolk is about a third of the egg, so its edge sits about 69 percent of the way from the center to the shell.

formula.text: Time = 27 × M^(2/3) × ln(0.76 × (Tegg - Twater) / (Tyolk - Twater)). For a large room-temperature egg at sea level, hard-boiled: 27 × 57^(2/3) × ln(0.76 × (20 - 100) / (84 - 100)) = 535 seconds, about 8 minutes 55 seconds.

howToSteps.name: Set the eggs out
howToSteps.text: Put the eggs on the counter about an hour before cooking, or in a bowl of warm tap water for 5 to 10 minutes. Do not leave them out for more than 2 hours.

howToSteps.name: Boil the water
howToSteps.text: Bring a saucepan of water to a full rolling boil while the eggs warm up.

howToSteps.name: Lower the eggs in
howToSteps.text: Lower each egg in gently on a spoon and start the timer at once. Room-temperature eggs crack less, but a spoon still helps.

howToSteps.name: Time it
howToSteps.text: Boil a large room-temperature egg for 8 minutes 55 seconds. A medium egg needs 8 minutes 10 seconds, an extra-large 9 minutes 40 seconds, and a jumbo 10 minutes 20 seconds.

howToSteps.name: Ice bath
howToSteps.text: Move the eggs straight to ice water for 10 minutes, then peel under cold running water.

title: How Long to Boil Room Temperature Eggs
tutorial: An egg at room temperature starts at about 20°C instead of the fridge's 4°C, and those 16 degrees save real time. A large egg needs 8 minutes 55 seconds to hard-boil from room temperature, against 10 minutes 10 seconds from the fridge. For a soft egg the saving is bigger in proportion: 3 minutes 20 seconds against 4 minutes 30 seconds.

Room temperature here means about 20°C, the convention Williams and most calculators use. A kitchen in summer might be warmer and a kitchen in winter cooler, but a few degrees either way moves the time by seconds, not minutes. If your eggs have sat out for an hour, use the room setting. If they just came out of the fridge, use the fridge setting even if the shells feel cool rather than cold.

Room-temperature eggs have a second advantage: they crack less. A fridge-cold egg dropped into boiling water gets a sudden shock as the shell warms unevenly and the air pocket inside expands. A room-temperature egg warms more gently. If you only ever boil fridge eggs, lowering them in on a spoon and pricking the wide end with a pin gives you most of the same protection.

The saving is not the same at every doneness. Hard eggs save about 1 minute 15 seconds, soft eggs save about 1 minute 10 seconds, and jammy eggs save about 1 minute 15 seconds. The starting temperature shifts the whole warming curve without changing its shape, so the saving stays near a minute whatever yolk you want.

One caution: do not leave eggs out all day to warm them. An hour on the counter is plenty, and the USDA says refrigerated eggs should not sit out for more than 2 hours. Set them out when you start thinking about breakfast, not the night before.
